title: Computing the 3-Edge-Connected Components of Directed Graphs in Linear Time
authors: Loukas Georgiadis (University of Ioannina, Greece), Giuseppe F. Italiano (LUISS University, Italy), Evangelos Kosinas (ISTA, Austria)
abstract: Let $G$ be a directed graph with $m$ edges and $n$ vertices. We present a deterministic linear-time algorithm for computing the $3$-edge-connected components of $G$. This is a significant improvement over the previous best bound by Georgiadis et al.~[SODA 2023], which is $\tilde{O}(m\sqrt{m}\,)$ and randomized. Our result is based on a novel characterization of $2$-edge cuts in directed graphs and on a new technique that exploits the concept of divergent spanning trees and $2$-connectivity-light graphs, and requires a careful modification of the minset-poset technique of Gabow [TALG 2016]. As a side result, our new technique yields also an oracle for providing in constant time a minimum edge-cut for any two vertices that are not $3$-edge-connected. The oracle uses space $O(n)$ and can be built in $O(m\log n)$ time: given two query vertices, it determines in constant time whether they are $3$-edge-connected, or provides a $k$-edge cut, with $k\le 2$, that separates them.

Connectivity-related problems are known to be much more
difficult in directed graphs than in undirected graphs (see,
e.g., [Gab16], [HRW20], [KT18]). Indeed, there is a fundamental difference in the structure of the cuts in the two
scenarios. Specifically, it has been established more than 60
years ago [GH61] that edge cuts in undirected graphs have a
nice structure, as defined by the Gomory-Hu tree (or cut tree),
which plays a special role in identifying, for any 𝑘, the 𝑘-edgeconnected components of undirected graphs. Furthermore,
many efficient algorithms for computing Gomory-Hu trees are
available (see e.g., [AKT21], [AKT22], [ALPS23], [CKL+ 22],
[HKP07], [LPS22]). On the contrary, in directed graphs edge
cuts have a more complicated structure, and it was proved
by Benczúr [Ben95] that in this case cut trees do not even
exist. It is thus not surprising that, while it is known how
to compute the 𝑘-edge-connected components of undirected
graphs in linear time for 𝑘 ≤ 5 [Gab00], [GI91], [GIK21],
[HT73], [Kos24], [NRSS21], [NI92], [Tar72], [Tsi09], the
situation is more challenging for directed graphs, where lineartime algorithms are only known for 𝑘 ≤ 2 [Tar72], [GIP20].

A. Flow graphs, dominators, and bridges
A flow graph is a directed graph with a distinguished start
vertex 𝑠 such that every vertex is reachable from 𝑠. Let 𝐺 =
(𝑉, 𝐸) be a strongly connected graph. Since 𝐺 is strongly
connected, all vertices are reachable from 𝑠 and reach 𝑠, so

𝑠. To avoid ambiguities, throughout the paper we will denote
those flow graphs respectively by 𝐺 𝑠 and 𝐺 𝑠𝑅 . Let 𝐺 𝑠 be a flow
graph with start vertex 𝑠. An edge (𝑢, 𝑣) is a bridge of 𝐺 𝑠 if
all paths from 𝑠 to 𝑣 include (𝑢, 𝑣).1 A vertex 𝑢 is a dominator

Its transitive reduction is a rooted tree, the dominator tree

The dominator tree and the bridges of a flow graph can be

Let 𝐺 = (𝑉, 𝐸) be a 2CLG with at least two ordinary

linear time
Our goal is to compute the strongly connected components

in the previous section. However, “linear” time here means
𝑂 (𝑛 + 𝑚), where 𝑛 and 𝑚 is the number of vertices and

Our goal is to compute the strongly connected components
of the labeling graph LG of 𝐺 𝑠 in linear time, as discussed
in the previous section. However, “linear” time here means
𝑂 (𝑛 + 𝑚), where 𝑛 and 𝑚 is the number of vertices and
edges, respectively, of 𝐺 𝑠 . Thus, we cannot apply directly on
LG a linear-time algorithm for computing strongly connected
components, because LG contains Θ(𝑚) vertices and possibly
Ω(𝑛𝑚) edges. Instead, we have to perform the computation of
the strongly connected components of LG indirectly, without
explicitly scanning all of its edges. To do this, we rely on the
framework developed by Gabow [Gab16] in order to perform
the same task for a different “labeling graph” (also denoted as
LG), whose structure is very similar to LG.
On a high level, the idea is to use Gabow’s path-based
algorithm for computing the strongly connected components [Gab00]. This algorithm works in a depth-first manner,
and it issues requests to a next_edge function on the adjacency list of every vertex under consideration. When provided
with an edge, it determines in constant time whether it must
initiate action in order to update its underlying data structures,
or simply do nothing, because this edge cannot provide new
connectivity information at this stage of the algorithm (and
up until its termination). This enables the user to properly
choose which edges to provide Gabow’s algorithm with – and
one can skip the edges that, based on structural properties
of the adjacency lists, will not make a contribution to the
computation.
What makes this idea applicable here, is the convenient
structure of the adjacency lists of LG. Specifically, the adjacency list 𝐿 (𝑒) of every vertex 𝑒 of LG (which is either
an edge of 𝐺 𝑠 or the copy of a special edge of 𝐺 𝑠 ) can be
partitioned into three types of sets of vertices of LG: (i) the
non-tree edges that are incoming to a vertex of 𝐺 𝑠 , (ii) a path
consisting of related vertices on 𝑇𝑖 , for 𝑖 ∈ {0, 1}, and (iii) the
copy of a special edge. (Note that types (i) and (ii) are due
to our considering special fundamental cycles: these can be
seen as the union of at most two paths that consist of related
vertices, plus at most two copies of special edges.)

Theorem V.7. For every digraph 𝐺 with 𝑛 vertices and
𝑚 edges, we can build a data structure with size 𝑂 (𝑛) in
